fact_text: When a trade war lowers global demand, oil and other commodity prices tend to fall, which benefits an importer like Pakistan; the analyst treats this as the main positive channel.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Tariff War & It’s Impact on Pakistani Market Explained' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lower oil and commodity prices shrink the current account deficit, ease pressure on the dollar and can lower interest rates, which the analyst saw as the transmission to Pakistan's market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Tariff War & It’s Impact on Pakistani Market Explained' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On some days, a flight to safety or panic selling can dominate, pushing stocks down regardless of the longer-term commodity benefit; such choppy periods tend to fade once trade positions become clear.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Tariff War & It’s Impact on Pakistani Market Explained' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A large part of the US trade deficit is financed by the rest of the world buying US bonds, since the dollar is treated as the safest asset with the least depreciation, so a change in that balance moves capital flows.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Tariff War & It’s Impact on Pakistani Market Explained' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A large exporter such as China takes time to shift capacity and orders to other countries, and the US runs a services surplus, so tariffs on goods alone limit the shock to the US economy in the analyst's view.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Tariff War & It’s Impact on Pakistani Market Explained' (YouTube transcript, undated)
